description: Renovate covers the Go modules, the GitHub Actions, the default container images, the base image of each Dockerfile, the Go toolchain, golangci-lint, helm, and the kind release.

One batch of updates arrives on one day. The window covers all of Monday, because a run that falls outside it creates nothing and leaves the batch waiting another week. The shared presets set no schedule.

customManagers.description: The container images a RedisFailover runs when it names none of its own. Each constant holds a tag and the digest it resolves to, and both move together.

packageRules.description: One pull request for a round of Go module updates. The module graph is nine direct requirements, few enough that reading them together costs less than reading them apart. A major arrives on its own, because a major is an API change to work through rather than a line to read.

The Go toolchain moves as one piece: the directive in go.mod and the builder image in both Dockerfiles. Every test job reads its Go version from go.mod. A builder image that moved alone would compile the operator with one toolchain and test it with another. The directive declares a minimum, so bump raises it rather than leaving it satisfied by a newer Go. The group takes no release-age delay, because a delay splits it. The shared preset exempts a bump, which is the update that raises the directive, and applies to the builder image, which is a patch. Docker Hub publishes the golang image after the Go release it carries. A delay therefore moves the directive on one run and the image on a later one. GOTOOLCHAIN=local in docker/app/Dockerfile then fails the build.

golangci-lint reads what the Go toolchain compiles, and a release older than the toolchain fails the lint job. It joins the toolchain group so that an update to both arrives in one pull request. It takes no release-age delay, for the reason the toolchain rule gives.

mockery carries its own copy of golang.org/x/tools to read the packages it generates from, so a release whose copy predates the toolchain cannot read what that toolchain compiles. It joins the toolchain group for the same reason golangci-lint does, and takes no release-age delay for the same reason. Unlike golangci-lint, nothing in CI runs mockery, so this pairing is what keeps the two together rather than a job that fails once they have come apart.

The Kubernetes code generators read what the Go toolchain compiles, so a generator compiled by an older Go cannot type check what this toolchain compiles. Go 1.27 added methods with type parameters and its standard library uses one, which a generator built by Go 1.26 rejects outright. The three join the toolchain group for the reason golangci-lint and mockery do, and take no release-age delay for the same reason. The development image compiles all three, so they travel with the builder image in that group rather than against it. Nothing in CI runs them, so this pairing is what keeps them together. See CIR-016.

The Kubernetes libraries take the patches of the minor they serve. A patch within that minor carries fixes and changes no API, which is why it arrives unattended. Renovate buckets a minor and a patch together and resolves the bucket to its highest release, so without this a reachable minor hides every patch behind it. This rule names no update type, which is what lets it apply before the lookup that does the bucketing.

The Kubernetes libraries hold the minor they serve. That minor is the API surface the operator compiles against, and the integration tests name the node images it has to run on, so moving it is a decision about which Kubernetes releases this operator supports. The move waits on the dependency dashboard rather than being dropped, so the decision arrives with the release. It groups apart from the module round, because a branch waits for approval when any update in it does.

kooper carries the Kubernetes libraries with it. v2.8.0 requires k8s.io/* v0.32.3 and v2.10.0 requires v0.35.0, so a kooper minor moves the API surface the operator compiles against. The rule that holds those libraries keeps Renovate from opening that move. It cannot stop a requirement forcing it. So kooper arrives on its own, where the move is the subject of the pull request rather than one line of a round.

The kind release waits on the dependency dashboard. Each kind release publishes its own set of node images, and the release notes pin them by digest, so moving kind moves the integration matrix and the Makefile default with it. Which Kubernetes releases this operator is tested against is a decision to make by hand, and docs/README.md names the matrix as the authority on it. Renovate does not watch the node images. kind never republishes a tag, so a new node image tag exists only because a new kind release exists, and an update that moved the images by themselves would pair them with the kind release the Makefile still names. The Kind image sync job in .github/workflows/ci.yaml holds that pairing.

Helm holds its major. Helm 4 changes the flags and the output of the command line. scripts/publish-oci-chart.sh reads the output of helm show with awk, and then packages and pushes a chart. That script runs on a release tag only, so no pull request reaches it, and a break there lands on a release. The move to Helm 4 is a change of its own, where the script runs against it first. It waits on the dependency dashboard, and it carries its own group. The GitHub Actions majors share a branch with it otherwise, and a branch waits for approval when any update in it does. Both names are here because the version input of azure/setup-helm reads helm, and a pin in the Makefile would read helm/helm.

go-redis publishes v9 under github.com/redis/go-redis/v9. The proxy serves those same tags under github.com/go-redis/redis/v9, the path this module requires. The go.mod inside each one declares the new path, so a major on the old path does not resolve. The move to v9 renames every import and changes the client API, so it is a migration to work through by hand.
One pull request for a round of default image updates. A digest that moves under an unchanged tag is a rebuilt image, and it rides along rather than opening a pull request of its own.

Redis takes the patches of the minor it serves. A patch within 7.2 carries fixes and keeps the license and the snapshot format this operator supports. Renovate buckets a minor and a patch together and resolves the bucket to its highest release, so without this a reachable minor hides every patch behind it. This rule names no update type, which is what lets it apply before the lookup that does the bucketing.

Redis holds the minor it serves. Redis 7.4 carries a different license, RSALv2 or SSPLv1 rather than BSD-3-Clause, and it writes a snapshot format that 7.2 cannot read back. Moving off this minor is a decision of its own, not one line of an image round. The move waits on the dependency dashboard rather than being dropped, so the decision arrives with the release. It groups apart from the image round, because a branch waits for approval when any update in it does.
